slides.title: Need for Disk Scheduling
slides.body: Need for Disk Scheduling

slides.title: Heading: Why Disk Scheduling
slides.body:
Subheading: Motivation And Need
Content:
Disk drives are shared across many processes, so several I/O requests are often pending at once for different cylinders. Because seek time dominates access time, the order in which these requests are serviced changes total delay sharply — so the OS uses a disk scheduler to choose that order rather than serving requests as they arrive.
Multiprogramming keeps many requests pending in the kernel I/O queue at once
Seek cost scales with cylinder distance, not with request count
Servicing nearby cylinders together cuts total head travel
Judged on total head movement, fairness, throughput and response time

slides.title: Heading: Scheduling Goals Metrics
slides.body:
Subheading: Judging Criteria
Content:
Every disk scheduling policy is judged against a common set of criteria, the same ones used later to compare FCFS, SSTF, SCAN and LOOK. These balance raw speed against fairness across all pending requests.
Total head movement — cylinders traversed to serve all requests
Average and maximum response time per request
Throughput — requests completed per unit time
Fairness — avoiding starvation of far-cylinder requests

slides.title: FCFS & SSTF
slides.body: FCFS & SSTF

slides.title: Heading: Scheduling Policy Landscape
slides.body:
Subheading: Four Algorithm Families
Content:
The order in which a disk services queued requests changes total head travel drastically for the same workload. Four broad policy families exist, ordered here from simplest to most seek-aware.
FCFS: serves requests strictly in arrival order
SSTF: always picks the nearest pending cylinder
SCAN/C-SCAN: sweeps across the disk like an elevator
LOOK/C-LOOK: sweeps but reverses at the last request

slides.title: Heading: FCFS Disk Scheduling
slides.body:
Subheading: Arrival Order Service
Content:
FCFS serves pending disk requests strictly in the order they entered the queue, applying ordinary arrival-order scheduling to cylinder numbers instead of CPU burst times.
No reordering: request distance from head is never checked
Head can swing across the full disk repeatedly
Trivial to implement: a plain FIFO queue
Wide swings inflate average seek time under scattered load

slides.title: Heading: SSTF Disk Scheduling
slides.body:
Subheading: Nearest Request First
Content:
SSTF always dispatches whichever pending request sits nearest to the current head position, trading arrival order for shorter seeks — the disk analogue of shortest-job-first scheduling.
Distances to all pending requests recomputed after every move
Selection needs a full scan of the queue each time
Far requests can starve while nearby ones keep arriving
Locally greedy per step, not globally optimal overall

slides.title: Heading: SSTF Disk Scheduling
slides.body:
Subheading: Analogy
Analogy:
A hospital nurse attends whichever patient's call bell is physically nearest, not whoever pressed it first — exactly as SSTF picks the nearest queued cylinder over the earliest queued one.

slides.title: Heading: SSTF Worked Trace
slides.body:
Subheading: Greedy Selection Steps
Content:
Using the same queue (98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67) and head at 53, SSTF picks the nearest remaining cylinder at each step instead of following arrival order.
Total head movement is 236 cylinders against 640 for FCFS on the identical queue, though request 183 — queued second — ends up served last.

slides.title: SCAN Family
slides.body: SCAN Family

slides.title: Heading: SCAN Family Overview
slides.body:
Subheading: Sweep-Based Scheduling
Content:
FCFS and SSTF either ignore seek distance or chase locality, both risking long waits for requests far from the current sweep. The SCAN family instead moves the head systematically across the disk in one direction, servicing every cylinder it passes.
SCAN: sweeps to one end, reverses direction there
C-SCAN: sweeps one way only, jumps back to restart
Both service cylinders in physical order, not arrival order

slides.title: Heading: SCAN Algorithm
slides.body:
Subheading: Elevator Movement Rule
Content:
SCAN moves the disk arm steadily toward one end of the cylinder range, servicing every pending request it passes en route. On reaching the last cylinder or the outermost pending request, direction reverses and the sweep continues the other way.
Service order follows cylinder position, not request arrival time
Requests behind current sweep direction wait for the return pass
Sweep restarts from the same end at every new cycle

slides.title: Heading: SCAN Algorithm
slides.body: Subheading: Diagram

slides.title: Heading: SCAN Algorithm
slides.body:
Subheading: Analogy
Analogy:
A lift travelling up serves every requested floor along the way before reversing at the top — just as SCAN sweeps to one end of the disk before reversing direction to service the rest.

slides.title: Heading: SCAN Drawbacks
slides.body:
Subheading: Uneven Wait Times
Content:
SCAN treats every cylinder fairly in movement order, but not in waiting time. A cylinder serviced just before a reversal waits almost a full sweep before the arm returns, while cylinders near the middle get serviced far more often.
Worst-case wait approaches nearly two sweep lengths for edge cylinders
Middle cylinders receive the most frequent, most even service
Arm may sweep to the disk edge even with no pending request there
Wait-time distribution is biased against the extreme cylinders

slides.title: Heading: C-SCAN Algorithm
slides.body:
Subheading: Circular Sweep Fix
Content:
C-SCAN, or Circular SCAN, removes SCAN's edge bias by treating the disk as a circular list. The arm sweeps in a single direction only; on reaching the last cylinder it jumps straight back to the starting end without servicing any request on that return.
Services requests in one direction only, for example low to high
Return sweep still counts as head movement despite serving nothing
Produces near-uniform wait time across all cylinders, including the extremes

slides.title: Heading: C-SCAN Algorithm
slides.body: Subheading: Diagram

slides.title: Heading: C-SCAN Algorithm
slides.body:
Subheading: Analogy
Analogy:
A canteen conveyor belt carries trays forward past students collecting food, then loops back empty underneath to the start — just as C-SCAN serves requests moving one direction, then returns unserved to begin the next sweep.

slides.title: Heading: C-SCAN Trade-Off
slides.body:
Subheading: Fairness Versus Distance
Content:
Treating the last cylinder as logically adjacent to the first turns the disk into a circular queue, so every cylinder waits roughly one full sweep between services. That fairness is bought with extra arm travel, since the return crosses the full range while serving nothing.
Wrap-around return usually spans more cylinders than SCAN's in-place reversal
Total head movement can exceed SCAN's for an identical request set
Predictable, near-equal wait suits latency-sensitive or real-time workloads
SCAN remains cheaper in raw seek distance for lighter, general loads

slides.title: Heading: SCAN Vs C-SCAN
slides.body:
Subheading: Head Movement Compared
Content:
Both algorithms sweep the head systematically instead of chasing arrival order or locality, but they differ in how they treat the boundary and how evenly cylinders get serviced.

slides.title: LOOK Family
slides.body: LOOK Family

slides.title: Heading: LOOK Family Overview
slides.body:
Subheading: Two Bounded Variants
Content:
SCAN and C-SCAN, covered earlier, always travel to the disk edge even when no request lies beyond the last one on that pass. LOOK and C-LOOK remove that wasted travel by reversing as soon as requests in the current direction run out.
LOOK: reverses like SCAN, skips the edge run
C-LOOK: reverses like C-SCAN, skips both edge runs
Both check the pending-request bounds before continuing
Named for the head checking ahead before moving further

slides.title: Heading: LOOK Algorithm
slides.body:
Subheading: Reversing Before Edge
Content:
LOOK behaves like SCAN inside the busy range of requests but stops sweeping the moment the queue ahead is empty, reversing there instead of continuing to cylinder 0 or the last cylinder.
Head moves toward one end, servicing requests met
Reverses at farthest pending request, not disk edge
Repeats sweep in opposite direction next pass
Reduces unnecessary travel versus plain SCAN

slides.title: Heading: LOOK Algorithm
slides.body: Subheading: Diagram

slides.title: Heading: LOOK Algorithm
slides.body:
Subheading: Analogy
Analogy:
A night security guard turns back at the last occupied room instead of walking to the empty corridor's end — just as LOOK reverses at the farthest pending request instead of sweeping to the disk edge.

slides.title: Heading: C-LOOK Algorithm
slides.body:
Subheading: Circular Without Edge
Content:
C-LOOK combines C-SCAN's one-directional sweep with LOOK's early reversal, so unnecessary travel to the disk edges is removed on both ends of the cycle.
Sweeps only toward increasing cylinder numbers, serving requests met
At highest pending request, jumps back without servicing enroute
Jump lands on lowest pending request, not cylinder 0
Uniform wait times, no long return sweep unlike C-SCAN

slides.title: Heading: C-LOOK Algorithm
slides.body: Subheading: Diagram

slides.title: Heading: C-LOOK Algorithm
slides.body:
Subheading: Analogy
Analogy:
A one-way loop train runs from the first station to the last active stop, then returns empty straight to the first station without stopping en route — exactly as C-LOOK jumps back to the lowest pending request without servicing cylinders on the way.

slides.title: Heading: LOOK Family Comparison
slides.body:
Subheading: Movement And Trade-offs
Content:
LOOK and C-LOOK inherit SCAN and C-SCAN's direction rules but trim the edge trips, trading a slightly more complex termination check for lower average head movement.
Extra check: farthest/lowest pending request tracked each pass
Savings are largest when the queue is sparse near edges
C-LOOK gives more uniform waits than LOOK, as C-SCAN does over SCAN

slides.title: Comparison & Practice
slides.body: Comparison & Practice

slides.title: Heading: Algorithm Comparison
slides.body:
Subheading: Six Side By Side
Content:
The six algorithms sit on a spectrum from raw movement efficiency to guaranteed fairness. No single algorithm wins on every criterion, which is why real systems pick based on workload.

slides.title: Heading: Why Trade-offs Exist
slides.body:
Subheading: Movement Vs Fairness
Content:
Minimising average movement and guaranteeing fairness pull in opposite directions. SSTF always jumps to the nearest cylinder, so a request sitting far from the busy zone keeps losing to closer arrivals.
SSTF starvation: distant request repeatedly outranked by nearer ones
SCAN edge bias: recently visited end waits almost a full sweep
C-SCAN and C-LOOK fix bias with one-direction service only
Heavy, spread-out load favours the SCAN family over SSTF

slides.title: Heading: Movement Setup
slides.body:
Subheading: All six algorithms
Content:
SSTF 236: lowest movement, but starves distant requests
LOOK 299: second-lowest movement, moderate fairness
C-LOOK 322: extra jump, most uniform wait time
SCAN 331: full sweep to edge in both directions
C-SCAN 382: edge sweep plus a full return jump
FCFS 640: highest movement, but perfectly fair order
